cards.claim: Existing augmentations and training approaches induce a significant discrepancy between the typical size of objects seen by the classifier at train versus test time
cards.conditions: Image classification tasks with data augmentation; typical training-to-test scenario without explicit resolution alignment strategy
cards.effect: This discrepancy degrades classification accuracy and creates a train-test mismatch that reduces performance
cards.evidence: Experimental validation presented through systematic comparison of augmentation effects across train-test resolution pairs
cards.quote: This paper first shows that existing augmentations induce a significant discrepancy between the typical size of the objects seen by the classifier at train and test time.

cards.claim: For a target test resolution, using a lower training resolution offers better classification accuracy at test time
cards.conditions: Target test resolution is fixed and known in advance; image classification on ImageNet; comparison across multiple training resolutions
cards.effect: Improved accuracy at target test resolution: 77.1% ImageNet top-1 with ResNet-50 trained at 128×128, and 79.8% trained at 224×224
cards.evidence: Direct experimental measurement on ImageNet with standard benchmarks
cards.quote: We experimentally validate that, for a target test resolution, using a lower train resolution offers better classification at test time.

cards.claim: Fine-tuning specifically at the target test resolution is an effective and efficient strategy to optimize classifier performance when train and test resolutions differ
cards.conditions: When training and test resolutions differ; fine-tuning is computationally cheap; network pre-trained at different resolution
cards.effect: Efficiently recovers and optimizes accuracy across resolution transitions; enables strong performance from small training images (e.g., 86.4% ImageNet top-1 for ResNeXt-101 pre-trained at 224×224 then fine-tuned for 320×320)
cards.evidence: Experimental validation showing that cheap fine-tuning at target resolution achieves state-of-the-art results
cards.quote: We then propose a simple yet effective and efficient strategy to optimize the classifier performance when the train and test resolutions differ. It involves only a computationally cheap fine-tuning of the network at the test resolution.
